endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (3) Backup and recovery—can AI systems be restored after ransomware or system failure? What is the RTO?

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether rehearsing AI fallback, backup, recovery, or incident response procedures, or keeping records of those tests, changes outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard of untested fallback. The recommendation rests on three voluntary frameworks that use "should" language.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements are expert frameworks, and they reflect consensus judgment rather than measured effects on downtime, recovery time, or patient harm.

All three endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether records show the contingency plan was tested, NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to practice incident response plans for harmful generated content, and the CHAI playbooks ask whether AI systems can be restored after ransomware and what the recovery time objective is. None of these sources creates a binding legal requirement.

No supplied study reports how often AI fallback procedures fail during real outages or what harm follows when they do. The hazard therefore remains a plausible failure mode that the frameworks describe, and its frequency and severity in clinical settings have not been measured in the material provided.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units that run scheduled AI failover drills, restore tests, and incident response exercises against those that do not. Such studies should measure time to safe manual workflow, recovery time relative to stated objectives, missed or delayed care during AI outages, and the staff time the drills require. Descriptive studies of how often untested AI fallback plans fail during real incidents would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. This leaves unknown whether fallback testing protects these patients during AI outages, and whether safety-net systems with smaller IT staffs can sustain the testing the frameworks describe.
